idiom_name: public event EventHandler<TEventArgs> / Action<T> with += and -=
implementation_notes: The C# event keyword turns the pattern into syntax: a delegate field whose subscription is restricted to += and -=, with EventHandler<TEventArgs> as the conventional shape and the raising class as the only code allowed to invoke it. The publisher null-checks the delegate and calls it once, which invokes every subscriber synchronously in registration order; identity of the subscribers is never visible to the publisher. It is the idiomatic in-process realization, and the framework's own controls, timers and HttpClient use it.
pitfalls: A subscriber that throws aborts the multicast invocation for the remaining subscribers; the event pipeline does not isolate failures.
Events hold strong references to their handlers: a lambda capturing a long-lived object keeps it alive until the handler is removed with -=.
Raising the event through a copy of the delegate field (or from a derived class without the protected raiser) subscribes to or notifies the wrong instance.

variants.name: IObservable<T> / IObserver<T> (Rx.NET)
variants.implementation_notes: The BCL's IObservable<T>/IObserver<T> pair (since .NET 4.0) replaces the delegate list with a subscription object: Subscribe hands the observer a provider, returns an IDisposable that removes it, and error and completion are explicit callbacks. Rx.NET adds the operators - filter, select, merge, throttle, observe-on - that a plain event cannot express, which is why stream-shaped notifications (DiagnosticListener, telemetry) use this shape. Choose plain events for simple in-process notification and IObservable when consumers need to transform or combine the event stream.
pitfalls: A hand-written IObservable<T> gets the contract wrong easily (re-entrant Subscribe, missing OnCompleted); use Subject<T>/Rx.NET or the framework's providers.
Forgetting to dispose the subscription leaks the observer exactly like an unremoved event handler.
Rx operators run on whatever scheduler the pipeline chose; without ObserveOn the subscriber executes on the producer's thread.
